summary.text: The Coriolis force is a pseudo-force that acts on objects moving within a rotating frame of reference, and in everyday use that frame is almost always the Earth.
On Earth it deflects moving objects to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere.
It is imperceptible for everyday motions, but it strongly shapes large-scale winds and ocean currents and is responsible for the rotation of cyclones.

facts.label: Named after
facts.value: Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis, in an 1835 paper

facts.label: Strongest deflection
facts.value: Near the poles, falling to zero at the equator

items.prompt: You roll a ball across your kitchen floor. Why doesn't Earth's spin visibly curve its path?

options.label: Buildings shield objects from Earth's spin
The effect is too tiny for short motions
It acts only on air and water

items.explain: For everyday motions the Coriolis force is imperceptible; it shows up only over large distances and long times.

items.prompt: A long-distance wind is deflected by the Coriolis effect. Where on Earth is that sideways push weakest?
items.explain: The horizontal deflection is greatest near the poles and decreases to zero at the equator.

items.prompt: North of the equator, air starts moving from high pressure toward low pressure. Which way does it tend to veer?

options.label: To the left of its path
To the right of its path

items.explain: Rather than flowing directly from high to low pressure, winds north of the equator tend to flow to the right of that direction.

items.prompt: Riccioli and Grimaldi reasoned that a spinning Earth should push a north-fired cannonball off course, and no such effect was detected. What did they conclude?

options.label: Cannonballs are too heavy to push

items.explain: They argued that rotation should create the effect, so failing to detect it was evidence for an immobile Earth.

items.prompt: The Coriolis effect was predicted in the 1600s. Why did nobody measure it until the 1800s?

options.label: It appears only near the poles

items.explain: Their reasoning was correct, but the effect is so small it was not measured until the 19th century.

items.prompt: Imagine a frame of reference that is not rotating at all. What happens to the Coriolis force there?
items.explain: In a non-rotating inertial frame the Coriolis force and the other fictitious forces disappear; they are only correction factors for rotating frames.
